To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the 31 cases of suicide and serious self-harm were all avoidable and that, in each of them, the nurses were at fault.
the 31 cases were all associated with a failure to follow the trust's policy on observation and that the policy was often inadequate.

there are significant numbers of incidents of suicide/self-harm in people receiving in-patient care; these are preventable; the majority of incidents occur in male patients between the ages of 21 and 50, and the majority of these are patients with a dual diagnosis of drug/alcohol and psychiatric problems; and there is considerable variation in the quality of policies and procedures regarding observation of patients, and this variation is associated with the occurrence of incidents.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the need to ensure that all in-patient units are staffed by appropriately qualified nurses, that all patients have a comprehensive assessment of their needs, and that there are robust policies and procedures in place to address the needs of patients with dual diagnoses, particularly those with substance misuse problems.
the identification of factors associated with the occurrence of suicide and serious self-harm in the inpatient setting.
the need to develop a more effective and humane approach to in-patient care in the NHS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the majority of these incidents were preventable.
the 31 cases in the audit are indicative of a system in need of urgent and fundamental reform.
the majority of incidents could be prevented by the adoption of a few simple measures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there was considerable variation in the care provided to patients and, in some instances, the care was not of an acceptable standard.

the majority of the 31 cases could be prevented, or the harm minimised, by a more consistent application of existing national guidance and policy, and by a more systematic approach to risk assessment and management.

there is a need for more systematic research and that, in the interim, there is a need to set national standards for the management of people with mental illness in receipt of care on in-patient psychiatric wards.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Department of Health needs to set standards and provide resources to ensure that they are met.
the majority of these deaths could have been avoided by the application of simple, common-sense measures.
there is a need to improve the way in which patients with mental health disorders are cared for, in order to prevent further tragedies and the associated legal action.
